intro: Cellos begin a long G-major melody above plucked bass notes, and Mahler lets it bloom into a set of variations. An oboe brings a second, sorrowing tune; near the end, the whole orchestra suddenly throws open E major.

sections.label: A · Cellos sing over plucked basses
sections.mNote: A G-major melody, with sustained violas beneath

sections.label: B · The oboe laments in E minor
sections.mNote: A slower tune marked plaintive and very expressive

sections.label: A′ · Clarinets and violas enliven the tune
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns with quicker notes

sections.label: B′ · Cor anglais joins the lament
sections.mNote: The sorrowing melody returns in G minor

sections.label: A″ · The cello tune starts to dance
sections.mNote: Andante gives way to sudden, quick variations

sections.label: Coda · E major floods the orchestra
sections.mNote: Sweeping strings and harp, then a broad brass tune

cues.title: A song low in the strings
cues.text: Divided cellos sing in G major above a gently plucked bass line. The violas hold the harmony; violins and winds wait. Mahler marks the cello melody sehr gesangvoll — very songful — and lets it unfold without hurrying.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, printed p. 304: divided cellos, sustained violas and pizzicato basses. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The oboe adds another line
cues.text: The melody rises into the violins. An oboe adds a quiet, independent line above it, marked zart, tender. The basses keep their plucked tread beneath music that is growing steadily more airborne.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 304, rehearsal 1: oboe marked zart above the violin melody; pizzicato bass line continues.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Saint Ursula smiles
cues.text: Bruno Walter offers “Saint Ursula Laughs As Well” as a possible title for this movement. He explains that the saint’s solemn face carries a smile. His letter, written at Mahler’s request in December 1901, imagines that smile beneath the music’s sorrow.
cues.evidence: Walter to Ludwig Schiedermair, 5 December 1901, quoted and discussed by Bettie Jo Basinger: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: The oboe’s E-minor lament
cues.text: The pace becomes much slower. An oboe begins the second theme in E minor, accompanied by bassoon and horn, with a direction to sound plaintive and deeply expressive. The violins then take over the tune and carry it towards a brass-filled climax.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 306–308, rehearsal 2: Viel langsamer, oboe klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll, bassoon and horn accompaniment, then violins singend. E-minor second theme: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first tune grows lighter
cues.text: Clarinets and violas bring back the opening melody in quicker notes. Cellos and double basses pluck underneath. Mahler asks for graceful motion, beginning very moderately and becoming gradually livelier as the variation unfolds.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 309, rehearsal 4: Anmuthig bewegt, clarinet and viola melody, pizzicato cellos and basses; instruction to begin very moderately and move gradually faster.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two reeds share the lament
cues.text: The lament returns in G minor, now shared by oboe and cor anglais. Their dark lines overlap above quiet horns. The return is brief at first, then the strings take up the sorrowing tune and drive it to a larger outburst.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 314, rehearsal 6: Langsam, oboe and cor anglais with horns. G-minor return and its expansion: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The melody learns to dance
cues.text: Cellos recover the opening tune over plucked violas and basses. Then the metre abruptly changes to 3/8 and the strings begin an Allegretto. Further variations grow faster still, until Mahler reins them back into the slow melody.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 319, rehearsal 9: Andante, then Allegretto subito in 3/8 with an explicit instruction to change tempo suddenly; the following variations accelerate before Andante returns.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E major breaks through
cues.text: After the quiet return, E major arrives in a blaze of running strings, harp and timpani. Horns and trumpets lift up a broad melody from the finale. The song of heaven is suddenly here, a movement before the soprano can sing it.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 324–326, rehearsal 12 onwards: E-major outburst, running strings and harp, then Pesante brass melody. Its relation to the finale is described at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violins turn to harmonics
cues.text: The great brass sound has gone. Violins divide into four parts and play high harmonics above soft winds and harp. The final instruction is Gänzlich ersterbend — dying away completely. Mahler leaves only the thinnest thread of sound.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 327, final system: divided first violins in harmonics and Gänzlich ersterbend.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: An oboe opens E minor
transitions.from: A · Cellos sing over plucked basses
transitions.to: B · The oboe laments in E minor
transitions.how: The G-major music slows and dies away through muted strings and held wind chords. At Viel langsamer an oboe begins the E-minor lament over bassoon and horn. The strings remove their mutes while resting, ready to take up the new tune.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 306, rehearsal 2: morendo, Viel langsamer, oboe entry and Dämpfer ab in the resting strings.

transitions.title: Plucked strings restore the first tune
transitions.from: B · The oboe laments in E minor
transitions.to: A′ · Clarinets and violas enliven the tune
transitions.how: The lament’s closing phrases recede. Clarinets and violas recover the first theme over plucked cellos and basses at Anmuthig bewegt. Mahler keeps the underlying beat at first, then asks the variation to become gradually livelier.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 309, rehearsal 4 and its tempo instruction.

transitions.title: The oboe hands sorrow to cor anglais
transitions.from: A′ · Clarinets and violas enliven the tune
transitions.to: B′ · Cor anglais joins the lament
transitions.how: The first-theme variation dwindles through a solo violin phrase and quiet horns. An oboe begins the lament again; at Langsam, cor anglais joins it in G minor. The string accompaniment drops away, leaving the two reeds above soft horn chords.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 314, rehearsal 6: oboe pickup, cor anglais klagend and horn accompaniment.

transitions.title: The cellos recover their quiet tune
transitions.from: B′ · Cor anglais joins the lament
transitions.to: A″ · The cello tune starts to dance
transitions.how: The second lament dwindles to pppp. The cellos begin the first theme at Andante, with violas and double basses plucking beneath them. Clarinets enter later, before the sudden change to the quicker, three-beat variation.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 318–319, rehearsal 9 and the subsequent Allegretto subito.

transitions.title: A breath, then E major
transitions.from: A″ · The cello tune starts to dance
transitions.to: Coda · E major floods the orchestra
transitions.how: The slow theme settles into quiet, sustained chords. A marked breath separates them from the sudden E-major outburst: strings sweep up and down, harp arpeggios cross the orchestra and timpani reinforce the bass. Horns and trumpets then sound the finale’s broad melody.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 324–326: Luftpause before rehearsal 12, E-major key signature, then the Pesante brass phrase.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, III. Ruhevoll (Poco adagio), full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: Third movement, printed pp. 304–327, rehearsal figures 1–13: cello theme, oboe lament, variations and E-major coda.

timeline.note: Cellos, in two groups, sing the theme over sustained violas and plucked basses; the violins and winds are silent.
An oboe adds a quiet countermelody as the violins take the cello tune.
Divided violins float high; bassoons and horns support, with the harp touching in a few notes.
An oboe sings the E-minor lament over bassoon and horn; the resting strings remove their mutes.
The violins sing the lament while the lower strings and winds move beneath them.
Woodwinds rise to fortissimo above trembling strings and a climbing bass.
Horns and trumpets with bells raised drive the lament to its first brass climax; timpani roll beneath.
Clarinets and violas carry the livelier theme over plucked cellos and basses.
Cor anglais and oboe voice the lament; horns and low strings add soft harmony.
Full strings, wind chords and horns press the lament forwards over rolling timpani.
Clarinets, horns and soft timpani dwindle with the strings to pppp.
A bowed cello melody begins the final variation over plucked violas and basses; the clarinets rest and join later.
Violins and violas spin light figures in the sudden three-beat Allegretto.
Racing violins, piccolo and glockenspiel mark the Allegro molto.
Divided strings sing the slow theme tenderly above soft horns and clarinets.
E major breaks in: rolling strings, harp glissandi and a full wind and timpani tutti.
Horns and trumpets raise their bells for the broad melody, marked Pesante.
Harp and divided strings return to a whisper above the soft winds and horns.
Violins in four parts play harmonics high above soft winds and harp.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
